subject: Civil Engineering
title: Traffic Flow Theory
description: A 60-second lesson on Traffic Flow Theory.

hook.text: Traffic moves like fluid. Compress it too much and it stops — a jam forms.

buildup.text: Three variables define traffic: flow (vehicles per hour), density, and speed.

discovery.text: Flow equals density times speed. At maximum density, speed drops to zero — gridlock.

twist.text: Maximum flow happens at moderate density — not empty, not packed. The sweet spot.

climax.text: Greenshields' model describes this relationship — still used since 1935.

punchline.text: Traffic has physics, and engineers use it to design capacity.

quiz.question: What happens to traffic flow at maximum vehicle density?
options: Speed increases because drivers want to escape congestion
Speed drops to zero and flow stops — complete gridlock
Vehicles automatically reroute to parallel roads

details.summary: Traffic flow theory uses mathematical models to describe how vehicles interact on roadways by relating three fundamental variables: flow (vehicles per hour), density (vehicles per kilometer), and speed.
details.whyItMatters: Traffic flow theory underpins every highway design decision from lane widths to speed limits. Without these models, engineers could not predict when or where congestion would form.
takeaways: Flow equals density multiplied by speed in the fundamental equation
Maximum flow occurs at a critical density, not at the highest speed
Shockwaves explain how traffic jams propagate backward through traffic

faq.question: Why does traffic sometimes stop for no apparent reason?
faq.answer: Small speed reductions cascade backward through dense traffic as shockwaves. Each driver brakes slightly harder than the one ahead, amplifying the disturbance until vehicles stop completely. These phantom jams can persist long after the original cause disappears.

faq.question: What is the fundamental diagram of traffic flow?
faq.answer: It plots flow against density, showing that flow increases with density up to a maximum capacity point, then decreases as overcrowding forces everyone to slow down. The peak represents the road's maximum throughput capacity.
